doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: A Down Beat blindfold test and Charlie Parker's influence
summary: Carter respects the honesty of a critic's remark about one of his records; they defer the Parker discussion.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: While we’re on the subject of criticism, you had brought up before we started the interview today a recent piece in I guess it was Jazz Times or Down Beat, the blindfold test with Lee Conants [phonetic].
I think it was Down Beat.
Down Beat, in which they played for him one of your recordings.
And you said you appreciated . . . he sort of . . . well, maybe I’ll just let you say what he said then.

Well, I think that what he said and the honesty he expressed I was greatly impressed by, you know, and I’d say that I’ve always known him and liked him and appreciated what he did. I even respect him further because of his honesty, you know. So I don’t know what else there is for me to say about that. He said it, and I . . . you know.

Yeah. Well, actually, I think when we come to the forties and the Charlie Parker era and all that, we’ll read the quote and maybe discuss it then, actually, because it does pertain to the influence of Charlie Parker on soloists and on you in particular, or lack of influence, whatever. So I’d like to deal with that . . .
Well, the influence of Charlie Parker has been just unprecedented, really.
But I guess not enough, according to Lee. [laughs]
He didn’t mean that. No, no.
I know he didn’t mean that.
But we’ll read the quote again and get it exact and then . . .
